# PART 1 – The case and the vocabulary {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1 · 90 minutes
:::

::: notes
Part one. Why social science is argued about at all, in short; the matrix that separates reproducing from replicating; the five analysts who reanalysed the claim we work on today; and then the tools we use, in one slide, and getting everybody running before the break.
:::

## What are we doing when we do social science?

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is not private. It is offered to others so they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
That handover is the whole enterprise. Everything today is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
Start with the obvious question that nobody asks out loud. What are we actually doing? We are making claims about the world – claims that could turn out to be wrong, and that come with some statement of how we would find out. And a claim is not a private possession. You publish it so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it, and build on top of it. That handover is the entire enterprise. A finding nobody else can examine is not a contribution, it is an assertion. So when we ask today whether social science is in trouble, the question is really quite specific: does the handover work? Can someone else pick your finding up and do anything with it?
:::

## Three arguments that made people nervous {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments, in order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: put together small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and lots of teams chasing the same question, and you can show that most published findings in a field will be false without anybody breaking a single rule. Then Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn demonstrated it in practice – give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have, and you can push a five per cent false-positive rate above sixty. They proved it by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes you younger. And Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake: you do not have to run many tests for this to bite. If the one test you ran was chosen after you looked at the data, its p-value is already wrong.
:::

## And then people counted {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology experiments**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields, different designs, and in both **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
And then people stopped arguing and counted. The Open Science Collaboration took a hundred psychology experiments and replicated them properly – high power, original materials, the original authors consulted where possible. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result. Thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half the original size. That is the study that made 'replication crisis' a phrase outside methodology seminars. The second one is closest to home, because it is ours: seventy-three teams of sociologists and political scientists, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. Different fields, different designs, and the same uncomfortable conclusion. The finding depends on the finder.
:::

## It is not mostly fraud {.smaller}

::: {.small}
The mechanism is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these practices – not fraud, the ordinary kind [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person. That is exactly why the problem is hard: you cannot fix it by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
Now the important qualification, and I want to be emphatic about it. This is not mostly a story about fraud. Fraud exists and it is spectacular when it surfaces, but it is rare and it is not what these numbers are measuring. The mechanism is ordinary and it is structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small, individually defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data, because how else would you make them. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader sees one path through a garden with hundreds. And in most cases neither the data nor the code are available, so nobody can check any of it. John, Loewenstein and Prelec went and asked researchers directly, anonymously, with a mechanism designed to make truthful answers worth giving – and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. Not one of those steps requires a bad actor. Which is exactly why the problem is hard: you cannot solve it by hiring better people. [pause] So suppose you did hire the best people you could find, gave them all the same data and the same question, and watched. Somebody did exactly that.
:::

## Twenty-nine teams, one question {.smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the first many-analysts study. Every one since is a variation on it – including the one you are inside today.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
So let me show you the study that started all of this, because everything after it, including our own day, is a variation on its design. Silberzahn and colleagues, twenty eighteen. The question is deliberately concrete: are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones? The data went to everyone identically – two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the three thousand referees they had played under, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player-referee pairs, with skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who were not told the research question. And then the part that makes it a study rather than a survey: twenty-nine teams analysed it independently, reviewed each other's approaches before anybody had seen a single result, revised, and only then compared answers. Nobody could tune their method to get a number they liked, because nobody knew what number anyone was getting.
:::

## 'Replication' crises

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Another 'replication' crisis – terminological confusion?
:::
::: {.fragment}
The term 'reproducibility' has been used as a synonym for a number of different characteristics – reproducibility, robustness, replicability, repeatability, credibility, and trustworthiness.
:::
[[Successfully rerun the same code on the same data?]{colour="#b22222"}]{.fragment}
[[Re-analyse the same data a different way?]{colour="#1C69A8"}]{.fragment}
[[Collect fresh data and analyse it in the same way?]{colour="#4D179A"}]{.fragment}
[[Using the same data and same analysis but asking a different question?]{colour="#3C6301"}]{.fragment}
[[Asking the same question but answering it with fresh data and a different analysis?]{colour="#3BB8DB"}]{.fragment}
::::

::: notes
So: twenty-nine competent teams, one dataset, and no agreement. Now notice what I have carefully not said yet – what *kind* of failure that is. And that turns out to be the whole difficulty, because part of the problem is the word itself. For years 'replication' covered everything: rerunning someone's code, re-analysing their data a different way, collecting new data altogether. Those are three different operations, answering three different questions – but because we called them all 'replication', the crisis debates had people talking past each other for a decade. So before any numbers, we need vocabulary.
:::

## The data $\times$ analysis matrix


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](one-day-methods_files/figure-revealjs/matrix-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::


::: {.src}

:::

::: notes
Here is the whole framework on one slide, and if you take a single thing home today, make it this grid. The question stays the same throughout; what varies is the data and the analysis. Same data, same analysis – reproducibility: if I rerun your recipe, do I get your number? Same data but a different, justifiable analysis – robustness: does your finding survive my defensible choices? New data, same question – replicability. The fourth cell, new data and new analysis, is really generalisation, and we set it aside today. Sit with this for a moment – everything that follows this morning hangs off it.
:::

## Credibility is not truth

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.9; --lh: 1.15"}
**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated.

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence.
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms
:::

::: notes
The glossary is worth reading slowly, because it separates two things we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella: reproducibility, robustness and replicability as a family, all asking whether the answer survives repeating some step of the process. Credibility and trustworthiness are about how much confidence a finding deserves – and note the sentence in the middle. Because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth. A credible finding can be wrong. What credibility is built from is the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them. That last one is the one we will keep coming back to.
:::

## Quick check: credibility in the wild {.questionslide transition="fade-in none-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

- 'Reviewer 1' wants to ensure that your results are [reproducible]{.fragment .bounceIn}, so she sources your R script to run the entire analysis. You're in luck – she hasn't yet updated her `dplyr`, so the code runs.
- 'Reviewer 2' is very eager. He's unconvinced by your modelling choices, so he fits your data to another function to check if your findings are truly [robust]{.fragment .bounceIn}. You're in luck again – he recovers your point estimate to a reasonable precision, although the confidence intervals have widened.
- 'Reviewer 3' takes a special interest because he's just working on a similar paper on data they published recently. Do your results [replicate]{.fragment .bounceIn} when your methods are applied to that state-of-the-art dataset?
:::

## Quick check: credibility in the wild {.questionslide transition="none-in fade-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

'Reviewer 2' just doesn't want to let go...

- He tried a few alternative analyses of your data, including a fancy new regression method that he just released as an R package. His method gives results that are generally aligned to yours, but for the method to work, it would require a larger dataset; would your results really [generalise]{.fragment .bounceIn} to this new dataset published by 'Reviewer 3' that he just read about, if applying his new fancy method to it?
:::

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the plan, before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle. None of them is a general-purpose guarantee. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
So what does open research actually propose? Not a philosophy – a list of practices, and each one removes a specific, identifiable obstacle. Open data means someone else can re-analyse your evidence rather than taking your word for it. Open code means they can rerun your exact analysis. Open materials means they can run the study again in a new sample. Open access means they can read the thing at all, which sounds trivial until you try to get a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the plan before the results exist. And registered reports go further: the plan is peer-reviewed and the publication decision is made before anyone sees a result, which removes the incentive to find something. Each removes one obstacle. None is a general guarantee, and I want to be clear about that before we get enthusiastic.
:::

- A **published paper**, in full – no blinding: I could see the original estimates
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, lifted from the abstract
- A pointer to the **data** – in our case, sixteen Eurobarometer waves you fetch yourself from GESIS
- No instructions on method. Analyse it any way you can defend
:::

And two things I could not see: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.

::: notes
Let me show you what this was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was a published paper – the whole thing, not blinded, so I could see the original estimates, and if anything that pulls you towards the original answer. With it came the paper's central claim in a single sentence, lifted from the abstract, and a pointer to where the data lived. In our case that meant sixteen Eurobarometer waves that I had to go and fetch from GESIS myself, under licence. What did not arrive was any instruction on method. Analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout: who the other analysts were, and what any of them were finding. That isolation is the design – it is what makes the spread at the end mean something.
:::

## Two tasks, months apart {.smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit. Record one categorical conclusion: does the evidence support it?

::: {.fragment}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Months later, three instructions arrive that fix the question:

- use the **cosmopolitan** framing dimension as the outcome
- use the **unemployment rate** as the predictor
- **disregard** the contextual variables
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether we agree. Task 2 makes our *numbers* comparable – you cannot average five answers to five different questions.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion – does the evidence support it or not. Then months later, task two arrived with three instructions that pinned the question down: use the cosmopolitan framing dimension as your outcome, use the unemployment rate as your predictor, and disregard the contextual variables. Now, why run it in that order? Because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number – and you can only ask that second question once everyone is answering the same question, which is precisely what those three instructions manufacture.
:::

## How a hundred studies become one number {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports their test statistic and its degrees of freedom, in whatever form their model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so a Stata pooled model and an R multilevel model land on the same axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask: how far apart are five defensible answers?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising is what makes comparison possible – and it quietly assumes the five are estimating **the same quantity**. Hold that thought until Part 2.
:::

::: notes
So how do you compare a hundred studies analysed five ways each? Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, with its degrees of freedom – a t, a z, an F, a chi-squared. Those get converted onto a common scale: a partial correlation and a standardised mean difference, so that somebody's pooled Stata model and somebody else's R multilevel model can sit on the same axis and be read against each other. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all – so the spread you are about to see is a spread among analyses that passed review, not a spread that includes nonsense. And notice the assumption hiding in the conversion: putting five numbers on one axis takes for granted that they estimate the same quantity. Hold on to that. Part 2 is largely about what happens when they do not.
:::

Which brings us to the most useful question in quantitative research: what is your estimand? Lundberg and colleagues split the answer into three steps. First, the theoretical estimand: a unit-specific quantity and a target population, stated in plain words, before any model exists. Second, the empirical estimand: what in the observable data corresponds to that quantity – and making that link forces your identification assumptions into the open, which is exactly where the causal graph lives. Only third comes estimation, where R finally opens. When they audited a full year of papers in a top sociology journal, the unit quantity was clearly stated in five out of thirty-two. ## DAG crash course: three roles {.smaller}


::: {.cell}

:::

::: {.src}
X = predictor, Y = outcome. **Green** = the causal effect you want; **coloured** = the path you must reason about.
:::

::: notes
All the graph theory you need today, in three small pictures. In every panel the green arrow is the same thing – the effect you are actually after, X on Y. What changes is the coloured structure around it. A confounder is a common cause of your predictor and your outcome – that red fork is a back-door path, and if you leave it open you are biased, so you adjust to close it. A mediator sits on the causal path between them – the amber path is real, it is part of the total effect, so if the total effect is what you want you do not adjust for it, or you remove part of the very thing you are measuring. And a collider is caused by both sides – those edges are harmless until you condition on the collider, which opens a spurious path that was not there before. So the rulebook is short: adjust confounders, leave mediators alone for total effects, and never condition on a collider. That is the entire toolkit – the next four slides just give it a bit more depth before you use it.
:::

## Reading a DAG: open and closed paths {.smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](one-day-methods_files/figure-revealjs/backdoor-paths-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
Association flows along **every open path**, not only along the causal arrow. A fork or a chain is open until you adjust the variable sitting on it. A collider is the reverse: shut by default, and opened by the very act of adjusting for it.

- **Back-door criterion**: close every path that enters X from behind, keep the causal X → Y path open
- That adjustment set – and only that set – earns a causal reading
:::

::: {.src}
@HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat; @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch.
:::

::: notes
A DAG is read through its paths. Association does not only travel down the causal arrow – it flows along every open path between X and Y. So the job is to work out which paths are open and shut the ones you do not want. Two rules do all the work. A path through a fork or a chain is open, and you close it by adjusting the variable in the middle – that is the red back-door fork on the left. A path through a collider is the opposite: shut by default, and you open it by adjusting. The back-door criterion just packages this: close every path that sneaks into X from behind, leave the causal X-to-Y path alone. The set that does that – and only that set – is what you are allowed to read as causal.
:::

- **Total** = direct (green) + indirect (amber)
- Adjust for the mediator M → you estimate the **direct** effect only – a *different* estimand
- 'Control for everything' silently answers a question you never asked
- **Table 2 fallacy**: the other coefficients in your model are *not* all causal effects

## Fixed effects, the fast way {.smaller .deepdive run="r"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|3"}

m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes)
```

::: {.small}
The bar `|` separates the regression from the **fixed effects**. Everything after it is absorbed: `cntry` gives every country its own intercept, `year` gives every year its own.

The equivalent with dummies would be `mcosmo ~ unemp_c + factor(cntry) + factor(year)` – same estimate, 36 extra rows of output you do not want to read.

::: notes
This one you will type yourself in a couple of hours, so it is worth a slow look. Feols comes from the fixest package and fits linear models with fixed effects very fast. The bar is the key piece of syntax: everything to the left of it is the regression, everything to the right is absorbed as fixed effects. Country gives every country its own intercept, so we are comparing each country with itself over time rather than comparing countries with each other. Year gives every year its own intercept, so anything that hit all of Europe in a given year is soaked up. You could write the same model with dummy variables – the estimate would be identical – but you would get thirty-six extra rows of output that nobody wants to read. ## What those three instructions assume {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **'The cosmopolitan dimension'** assumes the five items form one scale, and that a mean of them is the right summary. A sum, a share, or a factor score would all be defensible
- **'The unemployment rate'** assumes the claim is carried by unemployment. The paper's own abstract says "poor economic performances" – which also names GDP growth
- **'Disregard contextual variables'** removes the country-level controls. That buys comparability and gives up any defence against a time-varying confounder
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these is wrong. Each one is a **decision**, made for you, that a different study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

::: notes

## Building a scale: mean, sum or share? {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Five binary items per respondent. Three defensible summaries:

- **Mean** of the five – a proportion between 0 and 1. Everyone contributes equally
- **Sum** – a count from 0 to 5. Same information, different scale, different coefficient size
- **Share** of all mentions – depends on how many options the respondent picked overall
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
These are not cosmetic. A **share** is relative to the respondent's own total, so somebody who ticked eight boxes contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. Mean and sum are not.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Among the five Multi100 analysts: one used a **mean**, one a **sum**, one a **share**, one three separate shares. All defensible; none the same quantity.
:::

::: notes
And how do you turn five binary items into one number? Three summaries, all defensible. The mean of the five, which gives you a proportion between nought and one and lets every item count equally – that is what our panel uses. The sum, which is a count from nought to five: the same information on a different scale, so the coefficient will be five times bigger and mean the same thing. Or a share of all the respondent's mentions, which is the interesting one, because it is relative to how many boxes that person ticked overall. Somebody who ticked eight options contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. The mean and the sum do not work that way. ## Four ways to handle countries and years {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
| Estimator | What it compares | What it assumes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pooled, clustered SE** | countries with each other *and* over time | no unobserved country differences |
| **Country FE** | each country with itself over time | country differences are stable |
| **Two-way FE** | the same, net of EU-wide year shocks | shocks hit everyone alike |
| **Random effects** | a weighted blend of both comparisons | country effects uncorrelated with the predictor |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
These do not answer the same question. Pooled asks whether *high-unemployment countries* frame the EU differently; fixed effects ask whether *a country frames it differently when its own rate rises*.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And it shows: of the 41 wrong-sign specifications in the cosmopolitan universe, **33 are pooled**.
:::

::: notes
Four estimators, and the thing to hold on to is that they do not answer the same question. Pooled with clustered standard errors compares countries with each other and with themselves at once, and assumes there is nothing systematically different about countries that you have not measured – which for twenty-seven European states is a strong assumption. Country fixed effects compare each country only with itself over time, which means every stable national difference drops out. Two-way fixed effects do the same and additionally soak up anything that hit all of Europe in a given year. Random effects blend the two comparisons, weighting by precision, and assume the country effects are uncorrelated with your predictor. Read the fragment carefully, because this is the substantive point: pooled asks whether high-unemployment countries frame the EU differently, and fixed effects ask whether a country frames it differently when its own rate rises. Different questions. And it shows – thirty-three of the forty-one wrong-sign specifications are pooled.

All it can do is put them next to each other – which is exactly what Part 2 warned you about.

## Reading a specification curve {.smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Five questions to ask any curve you meet, in any paper:

1. **What is on the vertical axis** – a raw coefficient, or something standardised? Are the signs aligned so that up and down mean the same thing throughout?
2. **How was the set built** – enumerated or curated, and by whom?
3. **Where does the published estimate sit** – at the median, or out at an end?
4. **Is the spread patterned** – does one axis produce the extremes, or is it scattered?
5. **What null is the significance shading against** – and are the specifications independent? (They almost never are.)
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
You are about to answer all five for your own curve. That is a publishable robustness section.
:::

**Description** – map how the estimate moves across every defensible choice. *(What we have been doing all day.)*

::: {.fragment}
**Inference** – ask whether the curve *as a whole* is surprising if there were no effect at all. *(A different, harder job.)*
:::

::: {.fragment}
The two are detachable, and most published curves stop at description.
:::
:::

::: {.src}
@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse; @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis
:::

::: notes
Last conceptual move of the day, and it is the one that separates careful readers of specification curves from impressed ones. A curve like ours does two different jobs. The first is description: showing how the estimate moves as the choices move – that is what we built, and it is genuinely valuable on its own. The second is inference: asking whether the curve, taken as a whole, is more extreme than you would expect if there were no effect at all. Those are different questions with different machinery, and they detach cleanly – Multi100 did the description without the inference, and so, so far, have we. The next three slides are about what the second job takes.
:::

## 840 estimates are not 840 tests

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Every specification re-uses the **same 270 country-years**. The estimates are deeply dependent.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
'63.9% significant' **describes** the curve. It is not a p-value for the claim.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Vote-counting across dependent specifications has no null distribution. You cannot tally the stars.
:::
::::

::: notes
The percentages set a trap. Sixty-three point nine per cent of our specifications are significant. It is very tempting to read that as evidence strength: "most tests pass, so the claim holds". But all eight hundred and forty specifications interrogate the same two hundred and seventy country-years. They share the data, so they share the noise: if sampling luck pushed a handful of country-years the claim's way, it pushed hundreds of specifications the same way at once. The percentage significant is a description of the curve, not a test of the claim. To test the claim at curve level you need to know what the whole curve would look like if there were nothing to find, and that null has to be constructed.
:::

## The permutation design {#building-the-nothing-the-permutation-design}

::: {.small}
- Break the one link that the claim needs: **shuffle each country's unemployment series in time** (jointly with growth), keeping everything else intact
- Refit **all 840 specifications** on each shuffled dataset · repeat **B = 500** times
- Compare the observed curve to the 500 null curves: is ours more extreme than chance produces?
:::

::: {.src}
The design is worked through in your inference reading; permutation inference after @PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues.
:::

::: notes
The null is built like this. The claim says a country's unemployment moves its EU framing over time. So take each country and shuffle its unemployment series in time – together with growth, so the macro side stays internally coherent – while leaving the framing data untouched. In a shuffled world the alignment between unemployment and framing is broken by construction: whatever curve you get is what pure chance produces on these exact data with these exact 840 specifications. Do that five hundred times, refit the entire grid each time, and you have five hundred ghost curves to stand ours against. If our curve sits in the far tail of those ghosts, the curve as a whole is evidence. If it sits comfortably among them – the description stands, but the inference does not.
:::

## How to read a curve-level test {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- With B = 500, the smallest reportable p is **2/(B+1) ≈ 0.004** – a floor, not a zero
- Near p = .05 the Monte-Carlo wobble is about **±0.01**, so treat p = .04 and p = .06 as the same finding
- [A DESIGN · NOT YET RUN]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – a curve-level test has to be fixed in advance, and this one has not been run; today we read the design, not a result
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Discussion (2 minutes, then chat):** the constrained cosmopolitan-only universe has 140 specs: **70.7% negative, 57.1% negative *and* significant.** Strong evidence? *Against what null?*
:::

::: notes
Two literacy points and then you argue. First: with five hundred draws, the smallest p-value the test can report is two over five hundred and one – about point zero zero four. That is a resolution floor, not a zero; more draws buy sharper floors at real compute cost. Second: near the point-oh-five boundary the Monte-Carlo wobble is around plus or minus point zero one, so a permutation p of point zero four and point zero six are the same finding twice. ## The multiverse has its critics {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. Today's grid is a **curated 840**, not billions, and the fork chart does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen

## "There is only one correct analysis" {.smaller}

::: {.small}
Lakens and colleagues push back hard, and the argument deserves to be taken seriously:

- A research question, **fully specified**, implies a quantity to be estimated
- That quantity, together with the design and the assumptions you are willing to make, implies **one analysis** that estimates it
- So a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate diversity. It is evidence that **most of those specifications are wrong** – they estimate something else
- On this reading, showing a wide curve is closer to an admission than to a robustness check
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Take it back to the red cards. Twenty-nine teams modelled one count of red cards as **linear, logistic or Poisson**. Those are claims about how the outcome was generated, and they cannot all be right – so on this argument the spread is not diversity, it is mostly error.
:::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
And now the strongest objection to everything I have just taught you, and I want to give it its full force rather than a straw version. Lakens and colleagues argue that a research question, once fully specified, implies a quantity to be estimated. That quantity, together with your design and the assumptions you are prepared to make, implies one analysis that estimates it. Not a family, one. From which it follows that a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate analytical diversity at all. It is evidence that most of those specifications are simply wrong – they estimate something other than what you said you wanted. And on that reading, publishing a wide specification curve is closer to an admission that you never specified your question than to a robustness check. That is an uncomfortable argument and I think it is largely right.
:::

## Which analysis, and how you would know {#how-would-you-know .smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Grant the argument. **One correct analysis exists.** Now: which one is it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Getting there needs the estimand *and* the identification assumptions *and* agreement about the measurement – and on this claim, reasonable people disagree about all three.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the curve is not a rival to the one-correct-analysis view. It is a **map of the remaining disagreement**, drawn because we cannot yet settle it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it points at what to argue about: on this claim, at the **outcome**, not at the estimator.
:::
::::

::: notes
So let us grant the argument. Suppose one correct analysis does exist. The immediately following question is: which one is it, and how would you know? To get there you need the estimand, and the identification assumptions, and agreement about how the construct is measured – and on this claim reasonable people disagree about all three, as you saw for yourselves this afternoon. So I do not think the curve is a rival to the one-correct-analysis view at all. I think it is a map of the disagreement that remains, drawn precisely because we cannot yet settle it. And read that way it is genuinely useful, because it tells you where the disagreement lives. On this claim it lives at the outcome – what 'EU framing' means – and not at the estimator, which is where the seminar argument would have been.
:::

## What preregistration settles {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does settle**

- That your specification was not chosen *because of* the result
- That your rule for what counts as support was written before you had one
- That a reader can see what you intended, and what you changed
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does not settle**

- Whether the specification was **any good**
- Whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies
- Whether the assumptions behind it hold

A badly-reasoned analysis declared in advance is still badly reasoned – now with a timestamp
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Which is why the estimand and the DAG came **first** today. Preregistration protects a choice; it is the causal reasoning that makes the choice worth protecting.
:::

::: notes
So where does preregistration fit? It settles a specific and limited set of things, and the two columns matter equally. On the left: it settles that your specification was not chosen because of the result it gave, that your rule for what counts as support was written before you had a result to bend it around, and that a reader can see both what you intended and what you subsequently changed. Those are real guarantees and no other mechanism provides them. On the right, what it emphatically does not settle: whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies, or whether its assumptions hold. A badly reasoned analysis declared in advance is still badly reasoned – it just has a timestamp on it now. Which is exactly why we did the estimand and the graph first this morning. Preregistration protects a choice. Causal reasoning is what makes the choice worth protecting.
:::
